theme: Vaccines, cancer & patient power · 백신과 환자

tracks.title: Could vaccines cure cancer?
tracks.note: 오늘 기사(환자가 소비자처럼 행동한다)와 같은 '건강·의료' 주제예요. 1회차는 대략적인 내용만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Hi Phil.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Hi Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Phil, have you had many vaccines in your life?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, these are injections to protect you from diseases.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Oh, I've had loads.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I had all the ones you have when you're a child, but I've also had some for travelling and working abroad so... yeah, I've had lots.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, many of us will have had vaccines to stop us getting common diseases such as flu or Covid 19, but could injections help us fight more complicated diseases too?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: In this episode of 6 Minute English, we'll be looking at some new research that has scientists very excited, and we'll be asking the question, 'Could vaccines cure cancer?'

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Let's start with a quiz question, Phil.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: There are lots of different types of cancer affecting many parts of the body, but according to the World Health Organisation, what is the most common cancer worldwide?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Is it: a) lung cancer, b) skin cancer, or c) stomach cancer?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Well, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I'm going to guess b) skin cancer.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, we'll find out the answer at the end of the programme.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Now, this idea of a vaccine that could cure cancer sounds really interesting.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Could you tell us a bit more about it, Georgie?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, scientists have been trying to develop a cancer vaccine for quite a long time.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If you think about many existing cancer treatments, such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy, these have quite a few side effects.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: But the idea is that a cancer vaccine would help the body's natural immune system help fight the disease, which could have fewer side effects and also be more effective.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Scientists are particularly hopeful about a new vaccine developed to treat skin cancer.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: BBC Radio 4 programme Inside Science has been hearing about the latest research.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Cancer cell biologist Anne Willis spoke to presenter Tom Whipple.

transcript.speaker: Tom Whipple
transcript.text: I guess this moment has been quite a long time coming, hasn't it?

transcript.speaker: Tom Whipple
transcript.text: There's been some false dawns in cancer vaccines.

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: I mean, there's been a lot of work in this space, and it's all been very encouraging, particularly in the animal models, but getting this to translate into humans can be a much harder, longer process, so it's very exciting that there's this breakthrough - apparent breakthrough - that's come through today.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Tom says that the development of the cancer vaccine has been a long time coming, and this means that it's taken a lot of time to achieve.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Tom also says there have been some false dawns, an expression meaning that something looks like it's improving when it's actually not.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Anne says there's been a lot of work in this space.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Space here means field of research - so, in this context, research into cancer vaccines.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Scientists think they might have made a breakthrough.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: That means they've made significant progress.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And Georgie, these vaccines that we're talking about, they aren't quite like the ones that we're all familiar with, are they?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: This isn't a vaccine to prevent you from getting skin cancer, is it?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The vaccine being tested is used to treat people after they've had a tumour removed.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: It's used to target any cancer cells that have been spread around the body, to stop the cancer from coming back, and the vaccine is made specially for each patient by looking at the cancerous cells in the tumour that's been removed.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Anne Willis explained more to BBC Radio 4's Inside Science.

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: So, cancer cells are very different from normal cells.

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: They contain lots of mutations.

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: So, you sequence the DNA of the cancer cell to work out how it's different from a normal cell.

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: And then, particularly for the bits of the cancer that's different on the surface of the cell, you take those bits of DNA and then you put them into the RNA vaccine, and then they'll make these bits of proteins that get recognised by the immune system.

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: So, it's a way of priming the immune system to the cancer.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Anne is saying that the scientists work out what in the cancer cells is different and put these bits into the vaccine.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The vaccine then becomes a way of priming the immune system to cancer.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If you prime something, you get it ready.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: The vaccine basically helps the immune system get better at recognising and fighting cancer cells in the body.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Now, that sounds like some really clever science here.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Could it make a big difference, Georgie?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, more trials are needed, but scientists are hopeful.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Here's Anne Willis again talking to Tom Whipple, presenter of Inside Science.

transcript.speaker: Tom Whipple
transcript.text: Are you excited?

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: Oh, I mean, very!

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: I'm just, you know... anything that will improve lives of cancer patients is always wonderful.

transcript.speaker: Anne Willis
transcript.text: And actually, seeing that this extraordinary technology is, sort of, starting to reach its promise - this is very exciting for everybody.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: So, Anne is excited.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: She says that after a long time working on this technology, it's starting to reach its promise.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And promise here means positive potential.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Phil, I think it's time I revealed the answer to my question.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I asked you, "What is the most common form of cancer worldwide?"

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: You said skin cancer, but the answer is actually lung cancer.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: In 2024, there were an estimated 2.4 million cases worldwide, according to the World Health Organisation.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with the expression a long time coming, which means something has taken a long time to achieve.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: A false dawn is when something appears to be improving, when it actually isn't.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Space can mean field of research.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: A breakthrough refers to making significant progress with something.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: If you prime something, you get it ready.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And promise can mean positive potential.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And that's bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Thanks for joining us and goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Bye.

quiz.answer: a) lung cancer. 2024년 WHO 추산으로 전 세계 약 240만 건이에요. 보너스: 오늘 나온 암 백신은 예방용이 아니라, 종양을 제거한 뒤 남은 암세포를 면역계가 잡도록 'prime'하는 개인 맞춤형 치료 백신이에요.

reading.title: Patients are acting more like consumers. Good
reading.summaryKo: 의료는 보통 보험사·의사가 결정하고 환자는 받는 쪽이라 시장이 비효율적이에요. 그래서 환자들이 챗봇으로 묻고, 스스로 검사를 시키고, 제약사가 직접 약을 파는 흐름이 커지고 있는데, Economist는 이 세 가지가 모두 반가운 변화라고 말해요. (앞부분만; 전체는 구독 로그인)
excerpt: The person who uses a product usually chooses it and pays for it. The great exception is health care. Most of the time insurers (public or private) decide what is covered; doctors decide what is prescribed and patients take what they are given. The result is markets riddled with inefficiency, and nowhere more so than in America, the world's biggest. This year Americans are expected to spend about $6trn on health, nearly a fifth of their country's gdp. Yet for all that money, about one adult in ten could not get an appointment when they needed one last year, and more than a quarter put off or skipped care because of the cost.

No wonder patients are taking matters into their own hands. They pepper chatbots with questions such as how to decode a blood test or prepare for an appointment; every week more than 300m people ask Chatgpt about health, says Openai, its creator. The market for tests that patients order themselves has grown to be worth about $4bn a year in America, double its size in 2021, reckons Morgan Stanley, a bank. And drugmakers have started selling directly to patients. Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical giant, now fills about half of new prescriptions for its obesity jab in America this way, bypassing insurers. All three developments are good news.
reading.tip: 부제 'Markets maketh medicine'은 성경체 말투(maketh)로 '시장이 의료를 만든다'는 말장난이에요. 임상검사실에서 일하시니 'decode a blood test', 'tests that patients order themselves'는 바로 써 볼 표현이에요. take matters into their own hands = 스스로 나서다.
